transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-23
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (AtlasOrbit Partnerships), Marcus Liu (AtlasOrbit CTO), Ravi Shah (AtlasOrbit Platform), Lena Ortiz (AtlasOrbit Security)

Auto-generated Summary: quick partner intro, high-level architecture options, security & commercial next steps (may be imperfect).

[00:00] Sara Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sara, AE on the partnerships team at Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Ellen Park: Hi, Ellen here, head of partnerships at AtlasOrbit.
[00:11] Marcus Liu: Marcus, CTO.
[00:13] Ravi Shah: Ravi, platform eng.
[00:15] Lena Ortiz: Lena, security.
[00:17] Diego Martinez: Diego, SE from Redwood. Priya with me too.
[00:22] Priya Rao: Hi all.

[00:30] Sara Kim: Great. The agenda — quick intros, why AtlasOrbit is exploring a reseller/marketplace route, then Diego/ Priya will walk through integration options: hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity integrations, and private VPC/on‑prem options. Then security & go‑to‑market mechanics and next steps. Anything to add?
[00:45] Ellen Park: Sounds good. We're mainly exploring two things: 1) a listed offering in our Atlas Marketplace where we can resell Redwood as a managed inference option to our ISV customers, and 2) a lighter technical co-sell where we broker customers to Redwood hosted API. We want to understand gaps and effort.

[01:05] Marcus Liu: I'll be focused on integration effort and network constraints. We operate an overlay network and have strict egress policies, plus some customers require on-prem connectors.
[01:15] Diego Martinez: Understood. High level, Redwood supports three deployment patterns: hosted API (fastest), Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools we can configure for reseller customers), and Redwood Private — VPC peering or an on‑prem appliance for fully private control. There are tradeoffs on latency, unit cost, and operational responsibility.

[01:40] Ravi Shah: When you say on‑prem appliance, is that something we ship into a customer's datacenter or more of a managed virtual appliance in their VPC?
[01:48] Priya Rao: Both patterns exist. For regulated customers we often do a private plane with an optional on‑prem runtime; otherwise VPC/private peering with customer‑managed infra + our control plane is common. The on‑prem package is heavier but removes egress concerns.

[02:10] Lena Ortiz: Security first — we need KMS options, HSM support, and audit logs. Also SSO and RBAC integration. What do you provide?
[02:20] Diego Martinez: We integrate with most major KMS providers, have HSM integrations for customers that require it, and you can bring your own keys. Audit logs and request-level tracing are part of Redwood Console. SSO is supported via SAML/SCIM and RBAC is configurable. I'll share the SOC2 and network diagrams.

[02:45] Marcus Liu: For the marketplace model, how are you thinking about revenue share and billing? Do we need to re‑bill via your API or can AtlasOrbit resell as a meter?
[02:57] Sara Kim: We have partner resale options. Typical flow: AtlasOrbit lists an offering (packaged model, e.g., base/plus/enterprise), customer signs through AtlasOrbit, and Redwood either bills via marketplace metering or we can invoice AtlasOrbit monthly for committed capacity. Pricing tiers affect margins — Diego will follow up with a sample pricing matrix.

[03:22] Ellen Park: For our ISVs, predictable throughput and SLA is a must. They don't want bursty throttles. Can you commit to reserved throughput for reseller customers?
[03:32] Diego Martinez: Yup, Redwood Dedicated is purpose‑built for that — reserved GPU pools, predictable QPS/throughput, can configure auto‑scale and burst policies. For resellers we can map customer accounts to dedicated pools or logical partitions, depends on scale. There is also routing logic so traffic can fall back to hosted variants if a dedicated pool is degraded.

[03:58] Ravi Shah: Are there quota or tenancy constraints when mapping dozens of customers? We have multi‑tenant models and some customers are noisy.
[04:06] Priya Rao: We recommend per-tenant isolation in Dedicated for noisy tenants. For smaller tenants, shared hosted with strict soft limits and per‑token costing is fine. We can add prefix caching and KV cache for repeated prompt patterns to reduce unit costs for high QPS tenants.

[04:34] Marcus Liu: Mentioned KV cache — will that require changes to our request flow? We currently proxy payloads through an edge layer.
[04:42] Diego Martinez: You don't need to change much. KV caching is handled at the runtime and can be exposed via policies; caching works best when you can provide consistent prompt prefixes or session tokens. We'll provide SDK snippets for common languages to glue it in.

[05:03] Ellen Park: On the technical side, we need a PoC: run a 24‑48 hour benchmark for typical customer workload (chat plus embedding workloads) and measure p95 latency, tokens/sec, and unit cost. Is that feasible?
[05:14] Diego Martinez: Absolutely. We usually do a 24h throughput run with representative traces. We'll need a sample workload, expected concurrency, latency SLOs, and desired model family (open model vs Redwood‑verified).

[05:30] Marcus Liu: We also want to test a private VPC peering scenario for one enterprise customer who requires no egress. How quickly can you stand up a VPC peering test?
[05:40] Priya Rao: For a test, we can set up a VPC peering environment in a couple of weeks, assuming network approvals and firewall rules are cleared. On‑prem physical appliance tests take longer and require scheduling.

[06:00] Lena Ortiz: A few security specifics: data at rest encryption, KMS key rotation frequency, Do you retain any customer data? What's your retention policy and ability to support short retention windows for some customers?
[06:11] Diego Martinez: Data at rest is encrypted by default, you can BYOK. Short retention windows are supported, and we have log export and purge controls. I'll share the retention matrix and SOC2/ISO certs.

[06:30] Ellen Park: From the go‑to‑market operations side, can we co‑brand labs or run joint webinars? And do you provide partner enablement kits?
[06:40] Sara Kim: Yes, we have an enablement kit, co‑branding guidelines, joint webinar templates, and a partner portal. We'll include those assets in the follow up.

[06:55] Ravi Shah: A quick technical question — what models do you recommend for an embedding first workflow vs a chat heavy workflow? Are you recommending quantized variants for cost savings?
[07:05] Priya Rao: For embeddings, we surface specialized embedding models optimized for vector quality; for chat we recommend a few model families depending on length and instruction tuning. Quantized variants (INT8/4) can provide significant cost reductions; we typically do a quality regression test as part of recommendations to ensure it meets customer thresholds. Redwood Optimize can profile workloads and suggest quantization levels.

[07:38] Marcus Liu: About PCI or other regulated workloads — have you done customers in payments or healthcare?
[07:44] Diego Martinez: Yes, we have customers in healthcare and finance. For high compliance we recommend Private with BYOK + HSM + audit log forwarding into customer SIEM. We can also do on‑prem appliances when necessary.

[08:02] Ellen Park: For the reseller split, would you expect an upfront commit or a revenue share on usage? What have you done historically?
[08:12] Sara Kim: Historically we do a mix. Small partners get a usage revenue share. For larger resellers/distributors we negotiate committed reserved capacity with a margin, and sometimes marketplace metering where AtlasOrbit gets a share of the metered revenue. We'll include sample structures.

[08:35] Ravi Shah: Network specifics again — do you support static egress IPs, and what's the recommended firewall setup?
[08:42] Priya Rao: We support static IP ranges for peering and firewall allow‑listing. For VPC peering we publish endpoints; for hosted API we support NAT/pool IPs. We'll share typical firewall rules and CIDR ranges.

[09:02] Diego Martinez: Quick note on telemetry: Redwood Console provides per‑route token cost breakdown, per‑model latency histograms, traces, and request traces with optional PII redaction. That helps partners instrument usage and cost to their customers.

[09:22] Marcus Liu: Regarding SDKs — do you expect us to embed Redwood SDK in AtlasOrbit orchestration, or call your REST endpoints directly? Any preference?
[09:31] Priya Rao: Either works. We provide language SDKs and REST APIs. For a white‑label reseller flow where AtlasOrbit re‑bills, many partners proxy requests through their own API layer and then call Redwood. For lower integration effort, direct SDK use with a partner token mapping is common.

[09:55] Ellen Park: Do you offer a marketplace listing template with required assets and compliance checklists?
[10:01] Sara Kim: Yes. We'll send a partner playbook and listing template. It outlines assets we need, badge guidelines, and the legal terms for marketplace metering.

[10:16] Ravi Shah: One of our customers wants model pinning and reproducibility — they require the exact model version used for inference to be frozen and auditable. Is that supported?
[10:24] Diego Martinez: Model version pinning is supported. You can lock to a model artifact and we keep lineage. We also have evals and quality monitoring if you want regression alerts when underlying variants change.

[10:43] Marcus Liu: How do you handle graceful degradation? If Dedicated pool is saturated, does traffic fail-open to a cheaper hosted model?
[10:51] Priya Rao: Yes, we have smart routing policies. You can define fallback chains — e.g., Dedicated -> lower-cost quantized variant -> hosted fallback. Policies can be per‑customer and respect cost/latency priorities.

[11:10] Ellen Park: For the pilot, we'd like to map three ISV customers: one low volume, one mid volume with embeddings, and one enterprise with strict security. Can Redwood support mixed deployment across those?
[11:20] Diego Martinez: Absolutely. Low volume on hosted, mid on shared hosted with caching, and enterprise on Private or Dedicated. We'll design the pilot matrices and acceptance criteria.

[11:36] Sara Kim: Action item recap — I'll send partner deck, pricing matrix, and partner playbook. Diego, you'll send test plan and security doc links. Lena, AtlasOrbit to share network constraints. We should schedule the technical deep dive week of 11/3.

[11:55] Marcus Liu: Sounds good. One more operational ask — do you provide sample SLA language we can include in our reseller agreements?
[12:02] Sara Kim: Yes. We'll include sample SLA and support escalation paths for reseller customers.

[12:12] Ellen Park: Great. Any final questions from the Redwood side?
[12:15] Diego Martinez: One quick one — for the benchmark, can AtlasOrbit provide a representative trace and desired p95 objectives?
[12:22] Ellen Park: We'll compile that and send it with the network constraints.

[12:28] Priya Rao: For the throughput test plan, also include any special prompt shaping or system prompt patterns — caching behaves differently with longer system prompts.

[12:36] Lena Ortiz: From security, we'll want a short list of required artifact formats: SOC2, pen test summary, encryption architecture doc. We'll send that to Sara.

[12:45] Sara Kim: Perfect. We'll wrap up and share the artifacts. Thanks everyone for the time.

[12:52] Ellen Park: Thanks — looking forward to the next steps.

[13:00] End of recording (note: timestamps after 13 minutes mark are approximate — meeting continued with minor Q&A and scheduling items through the 62 minute end).

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional speaker mislabels and short gaps. Some product names transcribed imperfectly (e.g., Redwood Dedicate vs Dedicated).
